Sources & data notes

BiblePath combines its original 157 curated profiles with a broad, disambiguated index of people from the Old and New Testaments. This is an expanding research collection, not a claim that every person, interpretation or family relationship has been captured.

STEP Bible

Expanded identity and genealogy data was created for STEP Bible, based on work at Tyndale House, Cambridge, and is used under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license.

The authoritative source is STEPBible/STEPBible-Data, specifically TIPNR — Translators Individualised Proper Names with all References. This build is pinned to commit ed476a8ee6e3f7b3a46fc48af6c7dabc02387b1d, retrieved on 21 October 2026. Individual profile and relationship sources link to the corresponding record in that snapshot.

What we changed

  • Selected named or title-identified human records. Place, group, deity, ambiguous person-or-town, synthetic anonymous bridge, historical-name-only and LXX-only records are omitted. References are restricted to the 66-book Protestant canon.
  • Preserved distinct identities for people with the same name. The original 157 BiblePath IDs and summaries are retained through an explicit, reviewed mapping.
  • Converted structured roles, names, parent and partner fields to the app format. New short descriptions use these structured fields. The source’s AI-generated Brief, Short and Article biographies are not imported.
  • Normalized biblical reference notation and linked imported name references to the ESV on Bible Gateway. Original curated passages retain their KJV links. The separate Bible reader uses the public-domain World English Bible, with its translation clearly labeled.
  • Omitted group/form word entries and LXX-only references. Some retained source name references can still concern a nation, descendant group, or another use of an ancestral name. They are presented as name references from the index, not independently verified quotations about the individual.
  • Omitted uncertain, indirect-ancestor, founder and descendant-group claims from direct parent lines. A flag in either the forward or reverse record suppresses the imported relationship.
  • Kept original verse-backed links and their notes. Added index-derived links with an explicit STEP Bible relationship-index citation, rather than presenting an arbitrary name reference as proof of a family relationship.
  • Corrected Lappidoth’s upstream gender field using Judges 4:4, and Deborah of Genesis 35:8’s role to Rebekah’s nurse. These corrections are annotated in their profiles and in scripts/person-overrides.json.
  • Omitted the source’s disputed Nahash identity from 2 Samuel 17:25, pending review. That verse names Nahash as Abigail’s parent, but does not establish the source’s identification of Nahash as Jesse’s wife and mother of his sons. Ten unsupported links are therefore omitted; the other three Nahash identities remain available.

Care with genealogies

Joseph’s relationship to Jesus remains explicitly legal parenthood. Heli is not assigned as Mary’s biological father. Disputed biological-parent interpretations for Jesus’ brethren, unproven spouse relationships, and selected ambiguous genealogical harmonizations are omitted. A missing line may therefore mean uncertainty or an import limitation rather than an absence of biblical evidence.

STEP Bible’s interpretation choices are useful research aids, but are not themselves the biblical text. Please follow the source links and compare the cited passages. The app distinguishes original passage-backed connections from imported index connections.

The complete Bible reader

The reader contains the 66-book Protestant edition of the World English Bible in American English: 1,189 chapters and 31,103 numbered verses. The text is public domain. World English Bible is a trademark of eBible.org. The official USFX source was retrieved on 22 October 2026; its SHA-256 is 6b95cc0f7207fe2a1805370d4db6121bbcdf809ec8609a8a3d91f063214a911b.

Verse wording and punctuation are retained, with whitespace normalized. Psalm superscriptions, speaker headings and source footnotes are preserved separately. Prefaces, cross-reference lists, word-tag metadata and noncanonical books are omitted. Some numbered verses have no main text in this edition; their source notes explain the textual variation.

Name links are BiblePath annotations, not part of the translation. They match names and aliases against the identity index, prioritizing identities indexed at that exact verse. Namesakes, possible name-only matches and collective names such as Israel are marked as ambiguous and offer a choice. A name link is a research aid, not a guarantee that every use refers to the selected individual. Spelling differences or missing index entries can leave a name unlinked.

Cities and towns

The cities explorer contains 604 named settlements with 4,125 indexed verse references. STEP Bible supplies the identities, name forms and biblical references. Settlement classification comes from OpenBible.info’s Bible geography data, licensed under CC BY 4.0, pinned to commit 7eb18a5ee62f27b9b93bd6689ea272d76dd23b8f. Individual records link to their source evidence. We selected and reformatted settlements, generated brief descriptions from structured reference fields, and omitted countries, rivers, mountains and ambiguous classifications. We did not import modern coordinates or source AI biographies.

Indexed city names can include poetic, regional and symbolic uses. Same-named or source-combined settlements carry notes where available. People listed beside a city are indexed in the same verses; that alone does not establish residence or physical presence. No endorsement by OpenBible.info is implied.

Connecting two people

The finder searches the entire people collection. It first looks for a directed ancestral route, then a reverse ancestral route, and then a shortest family route. Among equally short routes, it prefers more Bible-cited connections. The default searches only links with explicit biblical citations. Disabling that filter admits clearly labeled STEP-indexed links. Every displayed step retains its original source and notes. A missing route is an index limitation, not proof that two people are unrelated.

The Adam-to-Jesus example has 63 steps, combines the atlas’s selected genealogy accounts, and includes Joseph’s legal parenthood. It is not a claim to reproduce Luke’s genealogy or an uninterrupted biological lineage. Genealogy lists can omit generations.

Reproducibility

The local project includes scripts/import-tipnr.cjs, scripts/import-bible.py, scripts/import-places.cjs, original curated data, explicit identity mappings, exclusions, source checksums, and validation checks. The importers regenerate the deployable data files. Unmodified downloads are kept in an ignored local cache.

Credit: data from STEP Bible, CC BY 4.0; selected, reformatted and supplemented for BiblePath. Changes are documented above and in the import scripts. No endorsement by STEP Bible is implied.
